title: The Wall at Fort Julien: an Engineer of the Republic, Five Captivities, and the Stone He Handed Over
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Jura, the Republic, the Schools

stops.name: Orgelet, the joiner's youngest son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate follows the accurate Orgelet fix, 46.5217 by 5.6114, and not the variant pin about a kilometre southeast that circulates in the same research pool
stops.campa: In the Jura town of Orgelet, in a house of joiners and merchants, Pierre Bouchard and Pierrette Janet de Cressia have their seventh and last child on the twenty-ninth of April. They name him Pierre-François-Xavier. The father works wood, sells goods, and teaches; the family is neither poor nor noble, which in 1771 means the boy's road runs through schools rather than through regiments. The record of his birth is complete and the record of his commemoration is empty. Orgelet has never put up a plaque for him.
suggested_refs: The parish register of Orgelet, Jura, for 29 April 1771

stops.name: Orgelet, the collège through the rhetoric class
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources attest that he completed the collège of Orgelet through the rhetoric class but give no years, and the date here is a placeholder for his mid-teens
stops.campa: He goes up through the town's collège as far as the rhetoric class, the last rung the province offers: Latin, the ancients, the arts of argument laid out for boys who will become notaries and priests. The Revolution has not happened yet. Nothing in the curriculum of a Jura market town prepares a pupil for hieroglyphs, and nothing needs to. The man who finds the Rosetta Stone will find it as an engineer supervising masonry, not as a reader. Orgelet gives him the habit of finishing a course of study.
suggested_refs: The collège of Orgelet under the old regime

stops.name: Besançon, two years of philosophy and mathematics
stops.date_confidence: attested as two years at Besançon, dated in the pool to about 1789 to 1791; the month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: He crosses to Besançon and spends two years on philosophy and mathematics, and the second of these decides him. Mathematics in 1789 is not an ornament. It is the entrance to the corps of engineers and to the artillery, the one career in which a joiner's son can outrank a marquis. Bouchard leaves Besançon able to draw a fortification and calculate what will hold it up. Within four years the Republic will be short of that skill, and will take men who have it wherever it finds them.
suggested_refs: The collège of Besançon and its mathematics teaching on the eve of the Revolution

stops.name: Paris, sergeant-major of the Grenadiers
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources and defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At twenty-two he enlists in the Grenadiers de Paris as sergeant-major and marches with the armies of the Republic into Champagne and Belgium. The year is 1793: the levy in mass, the Terror, the frontier held by improvised divisions of men who six months earlier were apprentices. He serves as an infantryman before he serves as anything else, and the campaigns give him what no school gives, the sense of ground under fire. The corps of engineers takes such men gladly, because they have learned from the far side what a wall is for.
suggested_refs: The Grenadiers de Paris in the campaigns of Champagne and Belgium, 1793

stops.name: Meudon, the hydrogen and the eyes
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources and defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The Republic gathers its balloonists at the château of Meudon, where Nicolas-Jacques Conté runs the École Nationale d'Aérostatique and the hydrogen for the observation balloons is generated on site. Bouchard is admitted and promoted lieutenant of the aérostiers. During one of Conté's gas experiments an explosion damages his eyes. He keeps his sight and loses the balloons. Conté will surface again in Cairo five years later, working out how to print from the face of a stone that Bouchard has not yet pulled out of a wall.
suggested_refs: The École Nationale d'Aérostatique at the château de Meudon, under Nicolas-Jacques Conté

stops.name: Paris, the Hôtel de Lassay and Monge
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of November he enters the École polytechnique, then housed in the Hôtel de Lassay, and studies descriptive geometry under Gaspard Monge, who invented it. The school is three years old and is already the Republic's instrument for manufacturing engineers at speed. Monge will sail for Egypt with Bonaparte and sit as a founding savant of the Institut d'Égypte; his pupil will sail in the same fleet as a lieutenant of the génie. In the same Paris, René Haüy is teaching that generation to read structure inside stone.
suggested_refs: The Hôtel de Lassay, first home of the École polytechnique
Gaspard Monge's course in descriptive geometry

stops.name: Paris, the marriage of 23 April
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Three days after being attached to an expeditionary force whose destination nobody below Bonaparte is told, he marries Marie-Élisabeth Bergère, five years younger than himself. The wedding stands less than a month before he sails from Toulon. She will see him again in 1801 and then lose him to Saint-Domingue, to Spain, to England, and at last to Givet. She outlives him and receives from the King a pension of four hundred and fifty francs, a quarter of what he drew alive, for a marriage in which the two of them are rarely in the same country.
suggested_refs: The marriage record of Pierre-François Bouchard and Marie-Élisabeth Bergère, 23 April 1798

stops.name: Toulon, aboard the Franklin
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the embarkation; the fleet's sailing is dated in the pool to May 1798
stops.campa: He embarks at Toulon aboard the Franklin with the engineering corps of an armament whose object is a state secret. Bonaparte is twenty-eight. Aboard the same fleet ride Monge, Berthollet, Denon, and more than a hundred and fifty other savants with their instruments and their press in Arabic type. The soldiers believe they are going to England. Bouchard, a lieutenant of engineers with damaged eyes and a four-week-old marriage, is going to the single place on the map where his name will outlast him.
suggested_refs: The ship Franklin of the Toulon squadron, 19 May 1798
The Commission des sciences et des arts embarked with the expedition

stops.name: Valletta, the Knights give way
stops.date_confidence: attested to 10 to 12 June 1798; the middle day is used
stops.campa: The fleet puts into Malta and the Order of Saint John, sovereign on the island since 1530, surrenders it in two days. Grand Master von Hompesch gives up the Grand Harbour with almost no fighting. Bonaparte spends the following days abolishing the Order, freeing the galley slaves, and moving the treasury aboard, and then the convoy sails east again. For Bouchard the stop is a week at anchor. For Europe it is the moment a crusading order eight centuries old is dissolved by a general in a hurry to reach Egypt.
suggested_refs: The capitulation of the Order of Saint John at Valletta, June 1798
sources: English Wikipedia, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Alexandria, the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested; the fleet raised Alexandria on 1 July 1798 and the city fell on 2 July, all troops ashore by 3 to 4 July. One summary of Bouchard's life dates his landing to 4 July 1799, which is a year-typo: he found the stone at Rosetta in July 1799
stops.campa: On the first of July the fleet raises Alexandria, the city falls the next day, and the whole army is ashore by the fourth. Bouchard comes ashore with the génie, the corps of army engineers, one lieutenant among the specialists who will spend the campaign fortifying towns, digging wells, and clearing rubble the length of the Nile. He arrives a junior officer with no name attached to any discovery yet, one of hundreds Napoleon has brought to hold Egypt as much by masonry as by musket. His war will be masonry, and the masonry will be at Rosetta.
suggested_refs: The French landing west of Alexandria, 1 July 1798
sources: English Wikipedia, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Imbaba, the march on Cairo
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle; the coordinate is Imbaba on the Nile, where the fighting was, and not the Giza pyramid pin that circulates under the name of the battle
stops.campa: The army marches south along the Nile in July heat with Mamluk cavalry shadowing it, and meets Murad Bey's horsemen at Imbaba on the river bank, the pyramids visible some twenty kilometres off across the flood plain. The squares hold, the charge breaks on them, and Cairo's notables surrender the city the next day. Bouchard's engineering unit moves with the column. That he stands in the battle itself is not separately attested for him personally. The corps of engineers marches where the army marches.
suggested_refs: The battlefield at Imbaba on the west bank of the Nile, 21 July 1798
sources: English Wikipedia, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Cairo, the Institut d'Égypte
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Three weeks after taking Cairo, Bonaparte founds the Institut d'Égypte in a requisitioned palace and seats Monge, Berthollet, Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, and Denon in it as savants. The model is explicit: the Institut National founded in the Louvre three years earlier, among whose founding members sits the mineralogist René Haüy. Joséphine's husband is building an academy inside an occupation. Within a year this body will receive, examine, and print a stone that a lieutenant of engineers is about to stop a demolition party from breaking up.
suggested_refs: The founding session of the Institut d'Égypte, Cairo, 22 August 1798

stops.name: Fort Julien, the wall comes down
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved: the biography gives 15 or 19 July 1799, French sources give 19 July specifically, and Budge's 1913 account says August 1799. The earliest of the candidate dates is used and the others are recorded
stops.campa: Bouchard is ordered to Rosetta to rebuild the old fort the French have renamed Fort Julien, on the west branch of the Nile a few miles from the sea. Soldiers demolishing an ancient wall turn up a slab of dark stone, polished on one face, carrying three bands of writing: unknown signs at the top, another script across the middle, Greek at the bottom. He is a graduate of the polytechnique and he reads enough to see that three scripts on one slab means one text set down three times. He stops the demolition.
stops.quote: During these works he discovered the Rosetta Stone on 15 or 19 July 1799.
suggested_refs: Fort Julien, the Ottoman fort at Rashid rebuilt by the French in 1799

stops.name: Rosetta, the report to Menou
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the report to Menou is attested but not dated, and is placed here on the day after the earliest candidate date for the find
stops.campa: With Colonel d'Hautpoul, who commands the works, Bouchard reports the find to General Jacques-François Menou, then at Rosetta. Some retellings give the recognition jointly to the two officers. Budge, writing in London a century later, spells the finder's name Boussard, is unsure whether it was Bouchard at all, and believes he rose to general and was alive in 1814, by which date Bouchard was in fact a chef de bataillon coming home from an English prison. The find enters the record already contested.
stops.quote: The actual finder of the Stone was a French Officer of Engineers, whose name is sometimes spelt Boussard, and sometimes Bouchard, who subsequently rose to the rank of General, and was alive in 1814.
stops.quote_source: E. A. Wallis Budge, 'The Rosetta Stone' (1913 edition), Project Gutenberg 48649
suggested_refs: Budge's 1913 account of the discovery and its uncertainties
sources: E. A. Wallis Budge, 'The Rosetta Stone' (1913)

stops.name: Cairo, Lancret before the Institut
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Michel-Ange Lancret, member of the commission of sciences and arts, stands before the Institut d'Égypte and reports that a stone found at Rosetta carries three versions of one inscription, one of them in Greek. The savants understand at once what they are being told. Nobody in the room can read the top band and nobody will for twenty-three years. The Greek at the foot is a key any of them can already read. Bouchard is still at Rosetta with his masons, having done the one part of the work that required standing in the right ditch.
suggested_refs: Lancret's report to the Institut d'Égypte, 19 July 1799

stops.name: Cairo, the stone delivered
stops.date_confidence: attested as the middle of August 1799; the day is a placeholder for that phrase
stops.campa: Bouchard is given the task of bringing the stone up the Nile to Cairo and arrives about the middle of August. The savants copy it, take impressions, and argue over it. Conté, whose hydrogen burned Bouchard's eyes at Meudon five years earlier, works out how to ink the incised face and pull prints from the slab itself, so the text can travel to Europe as paper instead of as basalt. Two lithographers, described in Budge as citizens Marcel and Galland, are brought from Paris for the copying.
stops.quote: Bouchard est missionné pour conduire la pierre au Caire, où il arrive vers le milieu du mois d'août
stops.quote_source: French Wikipedia, 'Pierre de Rosette', section 'Redécouverte : une pierre « française »'
suggested_refs: Conté's printing of the Rosetta Stone from the incised face, Cairo, 1799 to 1800
sources: E. A. Wallis Budge, 'The Rosetta Stone' (1913)

stops.name: Cairo, the Courrier de l'Égypte
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1799; the day is not recorded and is defaulted to the first
stops.campa: The expedition's newspaper prints the first public notice of the find in September, unsigned. Its reporter writes that the stone offers great interest for the study of hieroglyphic characters and that perhaps it will at last give the key to them. That is the whole future of the object stated as a hope in a garrison paper, two months after a lieutenant of engineers stopped a demolition. English retellings often quote a line about the key that is an encyclopedia's own paraphrase and not the Courrier's words; the two are not the same text.
stops.quote: Cette pierre offre un grand intérêt pour l'étude des caractères hiéroglyphiques, peut-être même en donnera-t-elle enfin la clef.
stops.quote_source: Anonymous notice, Courrier de l'Égypte, September 1799, as given in French Wikipedia, 'Pierre de Rosette'
suggested_refs: The Courrier de l'Égypte notice of September 1799, first publication of the find

stops.name: El-Arish, the fort opened
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed to late December 1799; the pool's own placement of this capture in January 1800, at the collapse of the convention, reverses the sequence, since the fort fell before the convention was signed on 24 January 1800
stops.campa: On the Sinai road the fort of El-Arish, held by a French garrison of some two hundred and fifty men, is opened to the Ottomans when the garrison mutinies. Bouchard is taken prisoner there. The Convention of El-Arish, negotiated a month afterwards and providing for a French evacuation of Egypt, is then repudiated by Admiral Lord Keith, whose orders forbid any separate treaty and demand unconditional surrender. Accounts that blame Sidney Smith are wrong: Smith negotiated the convention and supported it.
suggested_refs: The fall of the fort of El-Arish, December 1799
The Convention of El-Arish, 24 January 1800, and Lord Keith's repudiation

stops.name: Damascus, forty-two days
stops.date_confidence: attested as forty-two days of imprisonment at Damascus following the El-Arish capture; the pool dates it to 1800, and the day here is a placeholder inside that window
stops.campa: He is carried north and held forty-two days in Damascus, a French engineer in an Ottoman city he has no business in, waiting on an exchange he cannot hurry. The old city that holds him is the one where, half a century later, the Emir Abdelkader will settle in exile, teach Ibn Arabi in the Umayyad Mosque, and arm his household to pull Christians out of a burning quarter. Bouchard sees none of that. He is released, returns to Egypt, and goes back to work on fortifications.
suggested_refs: The old city of Damascus under Ottoman administration, 1800

stops.name: Cairo, captain of engineers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the place within Egypt is not specified in the sources and Cairo is used as the marker
stops.campa: On the first of May he is promoted captain of engineers, ten months after the find and a few months after his release from Damascus. The army he serves in has been left behind by Bonaparte, who sailed for France in August 1799 and took power at Saint-Cloud in November while his engineers were still repairing walls in the Delta. Promotion in this army is a matter of surviving in place. No reinforcement is coming, and every fleet between Alexandria and Toulon is British.
suggested_refs: The French army of the Orient after Bonaparte's departure, 1799 to 1801

stops.name: Fort Julien, taken a second time
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is reconstructed from the British advance up the Rosetta branch in the spring of 1801 and is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The British land at Aboukir and work up the Rosetta branch of the Nile. Fort Julien, the fort Bouchard was repairing when he found the stone, surrenders, and he is made prisoner inside the same walls a second time. The stone itself is no longer in them. It has been in Cairo and then Alexandria for a year and a half, in General Menou's keeping, and its fate will be settled not by the men who found it but by a clause in a capitulation neither of them will sign.
suggested_refs: The British advance on Rosetta and the surrender of Fort Julien, spring 1801

stops.name: Marseille, the landing home
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He lands at Marseille on the thirtieth of July, three years and two months after sailing from Toulon, repatriated out of an army that is still capitulating behind him. He is thirty, with the eyesight the Meudon explosion left him. He has been captured twice in the East, and he has handed the scholars of Europe the object that will make Egyptology possible. Nobody on the quay is waiting to ask him about Rosetta. There is another expedition fitting out, and engineers are wanted.
suggested_refs: The repatriation of the army of the Orient to Marseille and Toulon, summer 1801

stops.name: Brest, the fleet for Saint-Domingue
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the fleet's departure from Brest; the pool's compression of embarkation and capture into a single 1801 entry is corrected here
stops.campa: The expedition for Saint-Domingue sails from Brest on the fourteenth of December, sent to put down the revolution in the richest colony France has. Bouchard goes with it as an engineer officer, four and a half months after landing at Marseille out of Egypt. He has been in France long enough to be a husband in fact rather than in name, and no longer than that. The Atlantic carries him to the far side of the world from the Delta, into a campaign that will consume its army by fever rather than by battle.
suggested_refs: The Saint-Domingue expeditionary fleet, sailed from Brest 14 December 1801

stops.name: Paris, a daughter born while he is at sea
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month, day, and the town within France are not given in the sources and are defaulted, with Paris used as the marker
stops.campa: A daughter is born to Marie-Élisabeth Bergère in France while her father is in the Antilles. He will see the child on his returns between campaigns, at intervals of years. She dies at thirteen, shortly before her father's own death in 1822, and she goes unnamed because the sources consulted do not give one. A son follows around 1807, dated in those same sources only as approximate. Bouchard's family exists in the record as a short list of other men's dates.
suggested_refs: The civil register entry for Bouchard's daughter, 1802, not located in the sources consulted

stops.name: Cap-Français, the fever colony
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the yellow fever is attested but undated, and neither the port nor the station within Saint-Domingue is specified in the sources. Cap-Français is used as the marker
stops.campa: He is stationed in the colony as a military engineer and contracts yellow fever, the disease that is destroying the expedition faster than any enemy in the field. The exact port and posting are not specified in the sources consulted, and Cap-Français, the colony's principal town and the army's base, stands here as a marker rather than as an attested location. He survives the fever. Most of the officers who landed with him do not, and the reinforcements sent after them die at the same rate.
suggested_refs: The yellow fever mortality of the Saint-Domingue expedition, 1802 to 1803

stops.name: Cap-Français, the surrender of the colony
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed to late 1803: the French position collapsed after Vertières on 18 November 1803 and the last troops left by the end of December. The pool's dating of this capture to 1801 is three years early and is corrected here
stops.campa: The French position collapses after the defeat at Vertières on the eighteenth of November, the last troops are evacuated or taken by the end of the year, and Bouchard is captured on the colony's surrender. Haiti will declare its independence six weeks later. He has now been made prisoner three times in four years: in Sinai by the Ottomans, in the Delta by the British, and in the Caribbean by an army of former slaves that has beaten the one Bonaparte sent against it.
suggested_refs: The evacuation of Cap-Français after Vertières, November to December 1803

stops.name: Kingston, parole in Jamaica
stops.date_confidence: the release on parole is attested to August 1804; the day is defaulted, and the place of internment within Jamaica is not named in the sources, with Kingston used as the marker
stops.campa: He is interned by the British on Jamaica and released on parole in August. The precise place of internment is not named in the sources consulted, and Kingston stands here as a marker and not as an attested location. Parole means his word that he will not serve again until he is exchanged, and he keeps it, because officers do. He is thirty-three. The war that will take the next ten years of his life, and hand him to the Spanish and then the English, has not started yet.
suggested_refs: British prisoner-of-war arrangements in Jamaica, 1803 to 1804

stops.name: Napoléon-Vendée, the works in the west
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sources place his construction work in the Vendée across 1805 to 1807 without detail, and the month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: Back in France he is set to construction work in the Vendée, including at the new town Napoleon is having laid out on a grid and named for himself, Napoléon-Vendée. It is peacetime engineering: roads, barracks, a town where a village was, in the province that rose against the Republic ten years earlier and must now be built into obedience. The sources place him here across 1805 to 1807 and give no detail beyond that. It is the longest stretch of his adult life spent inside one country.
suggested_refs: The founding and gridded plan of Napoléon-Vendée, later La Roche-sur-Yon

stops.name: Irun, the crossing into Spain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the seven years of Peninsular service beginning in 1807 are attested, but no crossing point or date is documented for Bouchard individually and the Bidasoa pass stands as the army's route
stops.campa: He crosses into Spain with the army sent through the Basque country toward Portugal, and does not come back for seven years. The Peninsular War will take him under Dupont, Soult, Masséna, and Marmont in turn, four commanders and four different collapses. The crossing itself is not documented for him personally, only the army's route through the pass. Everything after this point in his life is siege engineering, and the sieges he is inside are mostly the ones that fall.
suggested_refs: The Bidasoa crossing and the French entry into Spain, autumn 1807

stops.name: Bailén, the capitulation of Dupont
stops.date_confidence: attested; the fighting ran 16 to 19 July 1808 and the capitulation was signed on 22 July. The apparent conflict between the two dates in the sources is a battle and its consequence, three days apart, and not a contradiction
stops.campa: Dupont's corps, cut off in Andalusia and beaten over four days of fighting around Bailén, signs a capitulation on the twenty-second of July, and Bouchard is taken with the rest of it. It is the first surrender of a Napoleonic army in the field and it is heard across Europe within weeks. He is now a prisoner for the fourth time. The stone he found nine years earlier is on public display in Bloomsbury, and the men holding him in Andalusia have no idea who he is.
suggested_refs: The capitulation of Bailén, 22 July 1808

stops.name: Cádiz Bay, the hulks and the island
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and flagged as such: the fate of the Bailén prisoners is attested, but whether Bouchard passed through the hulks, or was exchanged or paroled early, is not established in the sources consulted. Month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: Most of the prisoners taken at Bailén are held on hulks in Cádiz Bay, and many are then put ashore on the empty island of Cabrera, where thousands die of hunger over the following years. Whether Bouchard passes through the hulks, or is exchanged or paroled early, is not established in the sources consulted. He is fighting in Portugal within a year, which almost no Cabrera prisoner ever did. The bay marks the fate of his fellow captives; his own passage through it stays unrecorded.
suggested_refs: The prison hulks of Cádiz Bay and the deportation to Cabrera, 1808 to 1814

stops.name: Amarante, the bridge on the Tâmega
stops.date_confidence: the action at Amarante is attested to 1809 without a day in the sources consulted; the month and day are defaulted. The promotion to chef de bataillon that follows is attested to 24 November 1809
stops.campa: He distinguishes himself at the crossing of the Tâmega at Amarante during Soult's campaign in northern Portugal, on a bridge fought over from both banks. In November he is made chef de bataillon. This is the single action of his military career for which the sources record him personally distinguished, and it is a bridge. He has spent his working life on the engineering of crossings and walls, and the wall that made his name he was only rebuilding when the stone fell out of it.
suggested_refs: The bridge over the Tâmega at Amarante, contested in the spring of 1809

stops.name: Coimbra, the Portuguese campaigns and the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the service through Masséna's invasion and the campaigns of 1810 to 1811 is attested and the Legion of Honour is dated to 1811, but no engagement is named for him and the coordinate marks central Portugal as a theatre rather than an attested position
stops.campa: He serves through Masséna's invasion of Portugal and the campaigns of 1810 and 1811, and is made a Knight of the Legion of Honour. The specific engagements are not named in the sources consulted, and this coordinate marks central Portugal as a theatre rather than a place he is attested to have stood in. It is the fourth year of a war fought by starvation and demolition on both sides, in a country the retreating armies burn behind them, and engineers are the men who do the demolishing.
suggested_refs: Masséna's invasion of Portugal and the lines of Torres Vedras, 1810 to 1811

stops.name: Astorga, the garrison surrenders
stops.date_confidence: attested: the siege of Astorga ran 29 June to 19 August 1812 and the garrison surrendered on 18 August. Sources dating this capture to September confuse it with his shipment to England; sources dating it to 1810 confuse it with the earlier siege, in which the French were the besiegers
stops.campa: He is inside Astorga when Santocildes invests it in the summer, and the garrison surrenders on the eighteenth of August after seven weeks. He is captured for the fifth time and the last. The sources that date this capture to September have confused it with his shipment to England, and the sources that date it to 1810 have confused it with the earlier siege, in which the French were the ones taking the town from the Spanish. He is forty-one and has been a prisoner of three empires.
suggested_refs: The siege of Astorga, 29 June to 19 August 1812

stops.name: Portsmouth, shipped to England
stops.date_confidence: the shipment to England is attested to September 1812; the day is defaulted, and the depot or hulk that held him is not named in the sources. Portsmouth is an approximate marker, not an attested location
stops.campa: He is shipped to England in September as a prisoner of war and stays two years. The depot or hulk that holds him is not named in the sources consulted, and Portsmouth stands here as an approximate marker rather than an attested place. Ten years earlier, to this same coast, the captured French frigate Égyptienne had carried the Rosetta Stone into Portsmouth harbour as a prize of war. Bouchard arrives in England as cargo of the same war, and no record shows that anyone connects the two.
suggested_refs: The English parole towns and prison hulks holding French officers, 1812 to 1814

stops.name: Paris, home under the Restoration
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1814; the day is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: He comes home in July after the abdication, and the returned Bourbons make him an Officer of the Legion of Honour and a knight of the Order of Saint Louis. He is forty-three. He has served the Republic, the Consulate, and the Empire, and is now decorated by the monarchy that replaced all three. Close to a third of his adult life has passed in enemy hands. The stone he found is on public display in London, entered in the museum register as taken by the British Army, and nobody in Paris asks him about it.
suggested_refs: The First Restoration's confirmation of imperial officers, 1814

stops.name: Orléans, chief engineer
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is reconstructed from the sequence after his July return and is not given in the sources
stops.campa: He is appointed chief engineer of Orléans under the First Restoration, a post of settled provincial responsibility: the works of a city on the Loire, its bridges, its barracks, its stores. It is the first employment he has held in eighteen years that is not a war, and the first address at which his wife can reach him by post. He holds it less than a year. In March the Emperor lands at Golfe-Juan and the whole army has to choose again, and Bouchard, decorated by the King in July, chooses Napoleon in March.
suggested_refs: The engineering directorate of Orléans under the First Restoration

stops.name: Laon, the Hundred Days
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources and defaulted to the month of Waterloo
stops.campa: During the Hundred Days he takes part in the defence of Laon, on the rock above the plain that the roads to Paris cross. Waterloo ends it. He is put on half-pay, the standard treatment of officers who rallied to the Emperor, and for the first time since 1793 he is a man without a post. The King who decorated him a year earlier now has his name on a different kind of list. He is forty-four, and the record of the months that follow is too thin to say where he spends them.
suggested_refs: The citadel and plateau of Laon in the campaign of 1815

stops.name: Arras, the fortified towns of the north
stops.date_confidence: 1816 is the date the atlas follows; sources placing the reinstatement in 1815 contradict the half-pay of that same year, and two mutually exclusive states cannot share one year. Month and day are defaulted, and the coordinate marks the northern fortified belt rather than one attested town
stops.campa: He is taken back into the engineering service and attached to the fortified towns of the north, the belt of places on the Flanders frontier that France has walled and rewalled since Vauban. The sources that put this reinstatement in 1815 contradict the half-pay of the same year; 1816 is the date that leaves both facts standing. He works on walls again. He has worked on walls in the Jura, in the Delta, in the Antilles, and in Spain, and one of them had a stone in it.
suggested_refs: The fortified towns of the northern frontier under the Second Restoration

stops.name: Givet, death at his post
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate is the accurate Givet fix, and the fort of Charlemont stands on the promontory upstream on the left bank, not at the town-centre pin that circulates for this event
stops.campa: He dies at Givet on the Meuse, at his post as engineer in chief, after what the record calls a long and painful illness. He is fifty-one. His daughter, thirteen years old, has died shortly before him. His widow will be granted a pension of four hundred and fifty francs, a quarter of what he had drawn. No source consulted names the location or the form of his grave, and whether a marker was ever set over it is a gap in the record that nothing has filled.
suggested_refs: The fortress of Charlemont above Givet, his last command
The burial place of Bouchard at Givet, not located in any source consulted

stops.name: Alexandria, the stone surrendered
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the sources consulted give only 1801 for the Capitulation of Alexandria and the transfer of the antiquities, and the month here orders the event after Bouchard's 30 July repatriation
stops.campa: The French army in Egypt capitulates. Menou, who has claimed the stone as personal property, loses that argument, and the antiquities of the expedition pass to the British under an article of the surrender. Bouchard has been back in France for a month and takes no part in it. From this point the object and the man who found it have separate histories, and only one of them is written down at length. Conté's printed copies are already in Europe, so the reading does not wait on who owns the basalt.
suggested_refs: Article 16 of the Capitulation of Alexandria and the transfer of the antiquities, 1801

stops.name: Portsmouth, the Égyptienne comes in
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1802; the day is not recorded in the sources consulted and is defaulted
stops.campa: The stone reaches England in February aboard the captured French frigate Égyptienne, a French ship carrying a French discovery into an English port as a prize twice over. It is landed, shown to the Society of Antiquaries, and cast in plaster for the universities. Bouchard at this moment is in the Antilles with a fever. He will be brought to this same coast as a prisoner of war ten years later, and there is no evidence that anybody in England thinks of the two arrivals together.
suggested_refs: HMS Égyptienne and the landing of the Rosetta Stone at Portsmouth, February 1802

stops.name: London, the British Museum
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not given in the sources consulted and is defaulted
stops.campa: The stone enters the British Museum and has stayed on public display there ever since, the most visited object in the building. Painted lines on its flanks record that it was captured in Egypt by the British Army in 1801 and presented by King George III. The wall at Fort Julien, the demolition party, and the lieutenant of engineers who stopped them are not on the stone. A first complete translation of the Greek portion is published the following year.
suggested_refs: The Rosetta Stone in the British Museum, on display since 1802

stops.name: Paris, Champollion reads it
stops.date_confidence: the year 1822 is attested for the announcement; the month is a placeholder that orders it after Bouchard's death on 5 August of the same year, and the sources consulted give no day
stops.campa: Jean-François Champollion announces that he can read the Egyptian scripts, working from the Greek at the foot of the slab and from the copies Conté printed in Cairo. The year is 1822. Bouchard has died at Givet in August, aged fifty-one, and Champollion has ten more years to live, not twelve as one summary of Bouchard's life miscounts. The two men are joined by one object and by nothing else whatever. Neither of them ever writes a line about the other.
suggested_refs: Champollion's announcement of the decipherment, Paris, 1822

stops.name: Figeac, the replica in the other man's town
stops.date_confidence: not a dated event: the sources record the Kosuth replica at Figeac and the absence of any Bouchard monument as a present state of the record, with no installation date given, and the date field carries the date of compilation
stops.campa: At Figeac, the birthplace of the man who read the stone, the artist Joseph Kosuth has laid a giant black replica of the Rosetta Stone across a square as a floor, the largest commemoration of the object anywhere. No monument, statue, or plaque to Bouchard has been found at Orgelet, at Givet, or at Fort Julien in any source checked, and the location of his grave is unknown. The gap is what the record contains, and nothing has filled it.
suggested_refs: Joseph Kosuth's Rosetta Stone pavement at Figeac
The absence of any Bouchard monument at Orgelet, Givet, or Rashid
